title: Nervous and endocrine systems and how they coordinate organ systems
html:
How to use this sheet: you do not need any background to read it. Start with Key Terms. Each concept then goes: plain English → analogy → 3 core points → for every formula: what it says, when to use it, what each letter means, an everyday example, a step-by-step MCAT example and the trap → where to practice. Read top to bottom once, then use the formulas as a reference.

Key terms (read first)

TermPlain meaning
Cell / membraneThe smallest living unit / the thin, oily skin around it that controls what gets in and out.
IonAn atom with an electric charge. Body ions: Na⁺ (sodium), K⁺ (potassium), Cl⁻ (chloride), Ca²⁺ (calcium). The superscript is the charge.
Cation / anionA positive ion (Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺) / a negative ion (Cl⁻).
Concentration [X]How much of X is dissolved per liter. Brackets mean "concentration of". mM = millimoles per liter.
GradientA difference in amount between two places (more ions outside than inside). Things tend to flow from high to low, like heat from a hot cup to a cold room.
Voltage / mVElectrical "pressure" between two points / millivolt, one-thousandth of a volt (a AA battery is 1,500 mV).
ChannelA protein tunnel through the membrane that lets one type of ion pass. Voltage-gated channels open when the voltage changes; leak channels are always open.
Pump / ATPA protein that pushes ions "uphill" against their gradient / the cell's energy currency, which pumps spend.
ReceptorA protein that a specific signal molecule binds to, like a lock for one key; binding starts a response in the cell.
CNS / PNSCentral nervous system (brain and spinal cord) / peripheral nervous system (all the nerves outside them).
NerveA cable made of many axons bundled together.
NeuronA cell that carries electrical signals: dendrites (receive) → soma (cell body) → axon hillock (decides to fire) → axon (carries the spike) → terminals (release transmitter).
GliaSupport cells of the nervous system (myelin, nutrition, immune defense, CSF).
CSFCerebrospinal fluid: the clear fluid that bathes and cushions the brain and spinal cord.
Blood–brain barrier (BBB)Tightly sealed brain blood vessels that keep most substances in the blood out of the brain.
Membrane potential (Vm)Voltage inside the cell relative to outside, in mV. About −70 mV at rest in a typical neuron.
Equilibrium (Nernst) potential (E_ion)The voltage at which one ion's electrical pull exactly balances its concentration push, so it has no net flow.
Permeability (P)How easily an ion crosses the membrane (how many of its channels are open).
Depolarize / hyperpolarize / repolarizeMake Vm less negative / more negative than rest / return toward rest.
ThresholdThe Vm (≈ −55 mV) at the axon hillock at which voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open in a self-reinforcing burst.
Action potential (AP)The all-or-none spike that travels down the axon.
Graded potentialA small, local change in Vm whose size varies with the stimulus and fades with distance (EPSP, IPSP, receptor potential).
EPSP / IPSPExcitatory / inhibitory postsynaptic potential: a graded potential that pushes Vm toward / away from threshold.
Myelin / node of RanvierFatty insulating wrap on axons / the uninsulated gaps where APs are regenerated.
Resistance / capacitanceHow strongly something opposes current flow (Ω, ohms) / how much charge a membrane stores, like a small battery that must be filled before voltage changes.
SynapseThe junction where one neuron passes its signal to the next cell.
NeurotransmitterChemical released at a synapse that binds receptors on the next cell. ACh = acetylcholine, NE = norepinephrine.
Ionotropic / metabotropic receptorReceptor that is itself an ion channel (fast) / receptor that acts through a G protein and second messengers (slow, longer-lasting).
G proteinA switch protein inside the membrane that a receptor turns on; it then turns on enzymes.
Enzyme / kinaseA protein that speeds up a reaction / an enzyme that adds a phosphate tag to switch other proteins on or off.
Afferent / efferentCarrying signals toward the CNS (sensory) / away from the CNS (motor).
EffectorThe muscle or gland that carries out a response.
ReflexA fast, automatic response that does not wait for conscious thought.
Autonomic nervous systemInvoluntary control of organs: sympathetic ("fight or flight") and parasympathetic ("rest and digest").
GanglionA cluster of neuron cell bodies outside the CNS.
HomeostasisKeeping the body's internal conditions (temperature, blood sugar, salt, pressure) steady.
HormoneA chemical messenger secreted into the blood that acts on distant target cells that carry its receptor.
Endocrine glandAn organ that releases hormones into the blood (thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, pancreas).
Peptide / steroid hormoneA hormone made of a short protein chain (water-soluble) / one made from cholesterol (fat-soluble).
Second messengerA small molecule (cAMP, IP₃, Ca²⁺, DAG) that carries a hormone's signal inside the cell.
TranscriptionCopying a gene into mRNA, the first step of making a protein. Steroid hormones change it.
Tropic hormoneA hormone whose target is another endocrine gland (TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH).
Negative / positive feedbackThe output turns its own production down (stabilizing) / up (amplifying).
Half-life (t½)Time for half of a hormone or drug to be cleared from the blood.
Osmolarity / osmolalityTotal dissolved particle concentration per liter (mOsm/L) / per kilogram of water (mOsm/kg). Nearly equal in plasma; it sets which way water moves.
Glucose / glycogenBlood sugar, the main fuel / the stored form of glucose in liver and muscle.

A) CORE CONCEPTS

Concept 1: Neurons and glia

In plain English: Neurons are the cells that carry messages as electrical signals, each with an input end, a decision point and a long output cable. Glia are the far more numerous helper cells that insulate the cables, clean up and feed the neurons.

Analogy: A neuron is a company: the dendrites are the mailroom (input), the soma is headquarters, the axon hillock is the CEO who makes the yes/no decision, the axon is the delivery truck route, and the terminals are the loading docks. Glia are the support staff: electricians who insulate wires (myelin), janitors (microglia), and building managers (astrocytes).

Official definition: Neurons receive input mainly on dendrites and the soma, integrate it at the axon hillock, and transmit action potentials along the axon to synaptic terminals; glial cells (oligodendrocytes, Schwann cells, astrocytes, microglia, ependymal cells) support, insulate and protect neurons.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Input → decision → output. Dendrites receive; the axon hillock (lowest threshold, densest Na⁺ channels) adds up graded inputs and decides whether to fire; the axon conducts; terminals release transmitter.
  • The five glia. Oligodendrocytes myelinate many CNS axons each (destroyed in multiple sclerosis); Schwann cells myelinate one segment of one PNS axon; astrocytes support the blood–brain barrier and buffer (soak up) extra K⁺ outside neurons; microglia are resident immune cells (phagocytose, i.e. eat, debris); ependymal cells line the ventricles (fluid-filled brain cavities) and make/circulate CSF.
  • Neuron types and the BBB. Most CNS neurons are interneurons (connect neurons to neurons). Sensory neurons are pseudounipolar (one stalk that splits in two) with cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia. The blood–brain barrier favors small, lipid-soluble (nonpolar, oily) drugs.

Everyday example: Home wiring. Copper wire (the axon) carries the current; the plastic coating (myelin) keeps it from leaking. In the walls of the house (the CNS) one electrician coats many wires at once (oligodendrocyte); for the cords outside the house (PNS) each cord segment gets its own sleeve (Schwann cell).

Worked example (step by step): An autoimmune disease destroys myelin only in the brain and spinal cord, sparing peripheral nerves.

  1. Location = CNS only.
  2. CNS myelin is made by oligodendrocytes; PNS myelin by Schwann cells.
  3. Target = oligodendrocyte myelin (multiple sclerosis). In Guillain–Barré, which hits peripheral myelin, the target is Schwann cell myelin.

MCAT trap: Swapping oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells. "O" = One cell, many axons, CNS; Schwann = one cell, one internode, PNS.

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (dendrites receive), (axon hillock), (MS and oligodendrocytes), (Schwann cell), (astrocyte K⁺ buffering), (microglia), (ependymal cells), (crossing the BBB), (pseudounipolar sensory neurons), (interneurons).

Concept 2: Resting membrane potential: Nernst, Goldman and driving force

In plain English: A resting neuron is slightly negative inside (about −70 mV) because of how ions are spread across its membrane and which ones can leak through. Each ion has a "balance voltage" where it stops flowing (the Nernst potential), and the real voltage is a compromise among the ions, weighted by how leaky the membrane is to each. The gap between where the voltage is and where an ion "wants" it tells you which way that ion will flow.

Analogy: Each ion is a crowd pushing to leave a crowded room (concentration gradient) while a magnet (voltage) pulls it back. The Nernst potential is the magnet strength that exactly stops the crowd. The real membrane voltage is a "vote" among ions, weighted by how many doors (open channels) each one has.

Official definition: The equilibrium potential of an ion is the membrane voltage at which its electrochemical gradient (combined concentration and electrical push) is zero (Nernst equation); the resting membrane potential is a permeability-weighted average of the equilibrium potentials of the permeant ions (Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz equation), maintained over time by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (the sodium–potassium pump).

Core idea (3 points):

  • Rest sits near K⁺. At rest the membrane is most permeable to K⁺ (leak channels), so Vm (≈ −70 mV) sits near E_K (≈ −90 mV) and far from E_Na (≈ +60 mV).
  • The pump builds the gradients. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP. It builds the gradients (and adds a few mV directly, because it moves more + charge out than in) but is too slow to repolarize a single spike. Blocking it (with the drug ouabain) lets gradients run down over hours, so Vm slowly depolarizes.
  • Changing K⁺ or Na⁺. Raising extracellular K⁺ makes E_K less negative and depolarizes the resting cell (dangerous for the heart). If Na⁺ permeability suddenly dominates, Vm swings toward E_Na (this is the AP upstroke).
E_ion = (61.5 / z) · log₁₀ ( [ion]out / [ion]in )mV at 37 °C

In plain words: the balance voltage for one ion is 61.5 mV for every tenfold difference between its outside and inside concentration, divided by its charge.

When to use it: questions that give an ion's inside and outside concentrations and ask for its equilibrium (Nernst or reversal) potential, or ask what happens to E_K when blood K⁺ rises ("10-fold gradient", "equilibrium potential", "no net flux"). When it does not apply: it is for one ion at a time; for the actual resting voltage with several leaky ions use the Goldman equation. 61.5 is for body temperature (37 °C); at room temperature (25 °C) the constant is about 59 mV. Concentrations must be in the same units (both mM).

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
E_ionEquilibrium (Nernst) potential of that ionmV (inside relative to outside)The voltage that exactly stops net flow of that ion
61.52.303·RT/F at 310 K (R = gas constant, T = temperature in kelvin, F = charge per mole of ions)mVAbout 61–62 mV per tenfold gradient for a +1 ion
zCharge (valence) of the ionnone (+1, +2, −1)Divide by 2 for Ca²⁺; the sign flips for Cl⁻
[ion]out, [ion]inConcentrations outside and inside the cellmMRatio > 1 for a cation → positive E
log₁₀Base-10 logarithm: log 10 = 1, log 100 = 2, log 0.1 = −1noneEach tenfold ratio = one 61.5 mV step (for z = 1)

Everyday example: The decibel scale works the same way: loudness in dB = 10 × log₁₀(intensity ratio). A street that is 10⁷ times more intense than the faintest sound you can hear is 10 × 7 = 70 dB; each tenfold step adds a fixed 10 dB. In the Nernst equation each tenfold concentration step adds a fixed 61.5 mV (for a +1 ion), so a 1,000-fold gradient gives 61.5 × 3 = 184.5 mV.

MCAT worked example (step by step):

  1. K⁺: 5 mM out, 140 mM in, z = +1. Ratio = 5/140 = 0.0357; log = −1.447. E_K = 61.5 × (−1.447) = −89 mV.
  2. Na⁺: 145 out, 15 in. Ratio = 9.67; log = 0.985. E_Na = 61.5 × 0.985 = +61 mV.
  3. Ca²⁺ with a 10,000-fold gradient (more outside), z = +2: log = 4, E_Ca = (61.5/2) × 4 = +123 mV.
  4. Cl⁻ 10× higher outside, z = −1: log = 1, E_Cl = (61.5/−1) × 1 = −61.5 mV.

MCAT trap: Forgetting z. For Cl⁻ (z = −1), more ion outside gives a negative potential; for Ca²⁺ (z = +2) each decade is only ~31 mV. Also, the chemistry form at 25 °C (E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q, in volts) is the same physics at a different temperature and sign setup; do not mix the two.

Vm = 61.5 · log₁₀ [ (P_K[K⁺]out + P_Na[Na⁺]out + P_Cl[Cl⁻]in) / (P_K[K⁺]in + P_Na[Na⁺]in + P_Cl[Cl⁻]out) ]

In plain words: the real resting voltage is a Nernst-style calculation that mixes all the leaky ions together, each one counted in proportion to how easily it crosses the membrane.

When to use it: questions that give permeabilities (or say "the membrane becomes more permeable to Na⁺") and ask for, or ask which way, the resting or changed membrane potential moves. When it does not apply: it covers only ions that cross by leaking (it ignores the pump's small direct effect) and assumes a steady state. Ions with zero permeability drop out. Cl⁻ goes inside-on-top because its charge is negative; Ca²⁺ (charge +2) is not in this simple form.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
VmMembrane potential (Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz)mVThe weighted "vote" of all permeant ions
P_K, P_Na, P_ClRelative permeabilities (each compared with K⁺)none (ratios)Number of open doors for each ion
[ ]out, [ ]inConcentrations outside and insidemMCl⁻ terms are flipped (inside on top) because its charge is −1

Everyday example: Mixing bath water. Pour 9 cups of 10 °C water and 1 cup of 80 °C water: the mix is (9 × 10 + 1 × 80)/10 = 17 °C, close to the cold water because it has the bigger share. The membrane voltage is "mixed" the same way: K⁺ has by far the most open doors, so Vm ends up close to E_K.

MCAT worked example (step by step): Resting neuron: P_K : P_Na : P_Cl = 1 : 0.04 : 0.45; K⁺ 5 out/140 in, Na⁺ 145/15, Cl⁻ 110 out/10 in (mM).

  1. Top (numerator) = 1(5) + 0.04(145) + 0.45(10) = 5 + 5.8 + 4.5 = 15.3.
  2. Bottom (denominator) = 1(140) + 0.04(15) + 0.45(110) = 140 + 0.6 + 49.5 = 190.1.
  3. Vm = 61.5 × log(15.3/190.1) = 61.5 × (−1.094) = −67 mV, close to E_K because P_K dominates.

MCAT trap: Thinking Vm equals E_K. It sits a bit positive of E_K because of the small Na⁺ leak; raising P_Na drags Vm toward E_Na.

Driving force = Vm − E_ion

In plain words: the push on an ion is the gap between where the voltage is right now and the ion's own balance voltage; the bigger the gap, the harder the ion flows when its channel opens.

When to use it: questions asking which way an ion flows when its channel opens, whether a synapse is excitatory or inhibitory, or why no current flows at the reversal potential. When it does not apply: the sign reading depends on charge: for a cation, negative = flows in, positive = flows out; for an anion (Cl⁻) it is the reverse. It tells the direction and push, not the amount: no open channels = no flow, however large the driving force.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
Driving forceNet electrochemical push on the ionmVZero = no net flow even if channels open
VmActual membrane potentialmVWhere the cell is now
E_ionThat ion's Nernst potentialmVWhere the ion "wants" Vm to be

Everyday example: A room at 18 °C with the thermostat set to 22 °C: gap = 18 − 22 = −4 °C, so heat flows in. At 22 °C the gap is 0 and the heater stops, even though it is switched on, just like an open channel at E_ion carries no net current.

MCAT worked example (step by step): Vm = −70 mV, E_K = −89 mV, E_Na = +61 mV, E_Cl = −75 mV.

  1. K⁺: −70 − (−89) = +19 mV (positive, cation → K⁺ flows out).
  2. Na⁺: −70 − (+61) = −131 mV (negative, cation → Na⁺ rushes in, strongly).
  3. Cl⁻ (GABA-A channel opens): −70 − (−75) = +5 mV → for an anion this means Cl⁻ flows in and slightly hyperpolarizes, an inhibitory effect.

MCAT trap: Reading the sign the same way for anions. For a cation, negative driving force = influx; for Cl⁻, a positive driving force means influx. A channel open at exactly E_ion carries no net current.

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (rest near E_K), (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase stoichiometry), (raising extracellular K⁺), (ouabain), (Goldman and P_Na), (10× cation gradient), (Cl⁻ Nernst), (Ca²⁺ Nernst), (no net current at E_ion), (GABA-A and E_Cl).

Concept 3: The action potential and refractory periods

In plain English: When a neuron's voltage climbs past a trigger point, it fires a full-size electrical spike, the action potential, that races down the axon. The spike is always the same size; a stronger stimulus makes the neuron fire more often, not bigger. After each spike there is a short reset time when it cannot fire again.

Analogy: An action potential is a row of dominoes. A small nudge (sub-threshold) does nothing, but once the first one falls (threshold), the whole row falls with the same force no matter how hard you pushed (all-or-none). After falling, the dominoes must be set up again before they can fall again (refractory period).

Official definition: An action potential is a regenerative, all-or-none depolarization triggered when the axon hillock reaches threshold: voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open (depolarization), then inactivate while voltage-gated K⁺ channels open (repolarization and after-hyperpolarization); stimulus intensity is encoded by firing frequency.

Core idea (3 points):

  • The sequence. Threshold ≈ −55 mV → voltage-gated Na⁺ opens (depolarization to ≈ +35 mV) → Na⁺ inactivates (a plug closes the channel) + K⁺ opens (repolarization) → hyperpolarization (K⁺ channels slow to close). In voltage clamp (an experiment that holds Vm fixed and measures current) this shows as an early inward (Na⁺) current followed by a sustained outward (K⁺) current.
  • Refractory periods. Absolute (Na⁺ channels inactivated; no stimulus can fire a second AP) and relative (some Na⁺ channels recovered but K⁺ still open; a stronger stimulus is needed). The absolute refractory period makes conduction one-way.
  • Toxins and graded potentials. TTX (tetrodotoxin, pufferfish poison) blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ → no AP. K⁺ channel blockers → wider spike, slower repolarization. Graded potentials (EPSPs, receptor potentials) vary in size and decay with distance; APs do not.
Maximum firing frequency ≈ 1 / absolute refractory period

In plain words: a neuron can fire at most once per reset time, so the fastest firing rate is one divided by that reset time.

When to use it: questions giving the absolute refractory period and asking the highest possible firing rate, or asking how stimulus strength is coded. When it does not apply: it is a ceiling; real neurons usually fire below it because the relative refractory period also slows them. Convert ms to s first (2 ms = 0.002 s) to get Hz (spikes per second).

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
Maximum firing frequencyHighest rate at which APs can follow each otherHz (spikes/s)Ceiling on how loudly a neuron can "shout"
absolute refractory periodTime after a spike when no new spike is possibles (often given in ms)Reset time for Na⁺ channels

Everyday example: A subway turnstile that needs 2 seconds to reset after each person. At most 1/2 = 0.5 people per second, or 30 people per minute, can pass, no matter how big the crowd pushing.

MCAT worked example (step by step):

  1. Absolute refractory period = 2 ms = 0.002 s.
  2. Maximum rate = 1/0.002 = 500 Hz. With 1 ms it is 1,000 Hz.
  3. A stronger stimulus raises firing rate (toward this ceiling), not spike height.

MCAT trap: "The Na⁺/K⁺ pump repolarizes the neuron." Repolarization is due to K⁺ efflux through voltage-gated channels. The pump maintains gradients over the long run; it is too slow to shape a single spike.

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (repolarization), (absolute refractory period), (relative refractory period), (frequency coding), (TTX), (after-hyperpolarization), (voltage clamp currents), (one-way conduction), (graded vs. action potentials).

Concept 4: Conduction velocity, myelin and the length constant

In plain English: Signals travel faster down thick axons and down axons wrapped in myelin. Myelin works by stopping current from leaking out, so the signal can coast a long way and only needs to be re-boosted at the small gaps (nodes).

Analogy: An unmyelinated axon is a garden hose with leaks all along it; a wide hose loses less pressure per meter. Myelin is tape over the leaks, so the signal skips ahead from one gap (node) to the next, like a stone skipping across water (saltatory conduction).

Official definition: Conduction velocity increases with axon diameter (lower internal resistance) and with myelination, which raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance so current spreads passively to the next node of Ranvier, where Na⁺ channels are concentrated and the AP is regenerated.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Speed rules. Conduction speed rises with myelin (saltatory, "jumping", conduction between nodes of Ranvier) and with larger diameter. Velocity ∝ √(diameter) in unmyelinated axons and ∝ diameter in myelinated axons (∝ means "rises in proportion to").
  • Nodes do the work. Nodes of Ranvier are packed with voltage-gated Na⁺ channels; internodes (the wrapped stretches) have few. APs are regenerated only at nodes.
  • Why myelin helps. Myelin raises membrane resistance (r_m) and lowers capacitance, so less current leaks and less charge is needed to change Vm; the length constant grows and current reaches the next node.
λ = √( r_m / r_i )

In plain words: how far a signal can coast without a boost depends on how well the membrane blocks leaks compared with how hard it is for current to flow along the inside of the axon, and it grows with the square root of that ratio.

When to use it: questions asking how myelin, axon diameter or a membrane change affects how far a graded (passive) signal spreads. When it does not apply: it describes passive spread only, not the regenerated action potential. Because of the square root, a 100-fold change in the ratio changes λ only 10-fold.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
λ (lambda)Length constant: distance over which a passive voltage falls to ~37% (1/e) of its starting sizemmHow far a signal coasts without being boosted
r_mMembrane resistance for a unit length of axonΩ·cmFewer leaks (myelin) → larger r_m
r_iInternal (axial, along-the-inside) resistance per unit lengthΩ/cmWider axon → smaller r_i

Everyday example: A leaky hose. Make the hose wall 100 times less leaky and keep the inside the same: the distance the pressure carries grows by √100 = 10 times, not 100. Make the hose wider so water flows more easily along it, and the reach grows too.

MCAT worked example (step by step):

  1. Myelination raises r_m 100-fold with r_i unchanged: λ rises by √100 = 10×.
  2. Doubling diameter lowers r_i about 4-fold (cross-section ∝ d²) while r_m per length falls about 2-fold (more membrane around the circumference ∝ d).
  3. So r_m/r_i rises ~4/2 = 2× and λ rises ~√2 ≈ 1.4×.

MCAT trap: Thinking myelin speeds conduction by making APs "travel faster inside the myelin." No APs occur under myelin; they jump between nodes.

Conduction velocity = distance between stimulation sites / difference in latency

In plain words: speed is distance divided by time, but you use the time difference between two stimulation points so that the fixed delays (synapse, muscle) cancel out.

When to use it: nerve conduction study questions: a nerve is stimulated at two points and the muscle response times (latencies) are measured; find the speed. When it does not apply: do not divide by a single total latency, which includes synaptic delay and muscle activation time. Convert cm to m and ms to s to get m/s.

VariableMeaningUnitsIntuition
Conduction velocitySpeed of the AP along the nervem/sFast myelinated motor axons: ~50–60 m/s
distanceSeparation of the two stimulation pointsmPath the AP travelled
difference in latencyExtra time for the response from the farther sitesRemoves the shared synaptic and muscle delay

Everyday example: Timing a car between two streetlights 100 m apart with a stopwatch. Your thumb is slow by the same amount at both lights, so it cancels. If the car passes the second light 4 s after the first, speed = 100/4 = 25 m/s (90 km/h).

MCAT worked example (step by step): A motor nerve is stimulated at two points 20 cm apart; the muscle response latencies differ by 4 ms.

  1. Convert: 20 cm = 0.20 m; 4 ms = 0.004 s.
  2. v = 0.20/0.004 = 50 m/s.
  3. Unmyelinated scaling check: quadrupling diameter raises velocity √4 = 2×.

MCAT trap: Dividing distance by the total latency from one site. That includes synaptic delay and muscle activation time; use the latency difference.

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (APs regenerated at nodes), (axon diameter and speed), (myelin and membrane properties), (node of Ranvier membrane), (nerve conduction study).

Concept 5: Synapses and neurotransmitters

In plain English: Neurons pass messages to the next cell mostly with chemicals. The electrical spike arrives at the end of the axon, calcium rushes in, and tiny bubbles release a chemical that crosses a small gap and binds receptors on the next cell. Drugs and toxins often act by changing one step of this.

Analogy: A chemical synapse is a mailbox system: the electrical "phone call" (AP) arrives, calcium is the key that opens the mailbox, letters (transmitter) are dropped across the street, and the recipient reads them with a receptor. Clearing the mail (reuptake, enzymes, diffusion) ends the message.

Official definition: At a chemical synapse, depolarization opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels in the terminal; Ca²⁺ entry triggers vesicle (small membrane bubble) fusion and transmitter release; the transmitter binds ionotropic or metabotropic receptors, and its action is terminated by reuptake, enzymatic breakdown or diffusion.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Release needs Ca²⁺. Ca²⁺ entry triggers vesicle release (no Ca²⁺ outside → APs arrive but no transmitter is released). Botulinum toxin cuts SNARE proteins (the docking proteins that fuse vesicles) and blocks ACh release (floppy, flaccid paralysis). Electrical synapses (gap junctions, direct pores between cells) are faster, often two-way, and need no transmitter.
  • Receptor type decides the effect. Ionotropic receptors (nicotinic ACh, GABA-A, glutamate AMPA) are fast; metabotropic (G protein: muscarinic ACh, adrenergic) are slower and longer-lasting. The same transmitter can excite or inhibit depending on receptor (ACh: nicotinic on muscle excites; M2 muscarinic on the SA node, the heart's pacemaker, slows it). Summation: temporal (one input firing rapidly) and spatial (many inputs at once).
  • Ending the signal; key transmitters. Acetylcholinesterase breaks down ACh (its inhibitors prolong ACh action); NE and serotonin are mostly taken back up (reuptake; SSRIs block serotonin reuptake), then broken down by MAO (MAOIs raise these "monoamines"). Glutamate (main excitatory), GABA (brain inhibitory), glycine (spinal inhibitory; strychnine blocks it), dopamine (substantia nigra; lost in Parkinson disease), endorphins (bind opioid receptors, reduce pain).

Everyday example: A group chat. You send one message (the AP). It only goes through if you have signal (Ca²⁺). Friends read it only if they are in the group (have the receptor). If someone keeps scrolling back to reread it (blocked breakdown or reuptake), the message's effect lasts longer.

Worked example (step by step): Myasthenia gravis antibodies remove half the working nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction (nerve–muscle synapse).

  1. Same amount of ACh is released, but only half as many receptors respond.
  2. Each nerve impulse produces a smaller end-plate potential, so some muscle fibers fail to reach threshold → fatigable weakness (worse with repeated use).
  3. An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor lets each ACh molecule act longer and improves strength.

MCAT trap: Thinking curare and botulinum act the same way. Curare blocks the nicotinic receptor (postsynaptic); botulinum blocks ACh release (presynaptic). Both paralyze.

Practice in the 5,180 Qbank: (Ca²⁺ triggers fusion), (Ca²⁺-free solution), (temporal summation), (spatial summation), (AChE inhibitor), (SSRIs), (ionotropic speed), (botulinum), (curare), (glutamate), (strychnine and glycine), (Parkinson), (electrical synapses), (same transmitter, opposite effects), (NE reuptake), (MAOIs), (endorphins), (myasthenia gravis).

Concept 6: Organization of the nervous system and reflex arcs

In plain English: The brain and spinal cord are the control center; nerves are the wiring to and from the body. Sensory signals come in through the back of the spinal cord and motor commands go out the front. Reflexes are shortcuts handled by the spinal cord without waiting for the brain.

Analogy: The nervous system is a country: the CNS (brain and spinal cord) is the capital, the PNS is the road network. Afferent roads carry reports into the capital, efferent roads carry orders out. A reflex is a local mayor (spinal cord) answering urgently without waiting for the capital.

Official definition: The nervous system is divided into the central nervous system (brain, spinal cord) and peripheral nervous system (cranial and spinal nerves, ganglia); a reflex arc links a receptor, an afferent neuron entering the dorsal root, CNS integration, and an efferent neuron leaving the ventral root to an effector.

Core idea (3 points):

  • The reflex arc. Receptor → sensory (afferent, dorsal or back root; cell body in the dorsal root ganglion) → interneuron → motor (efferent, ventral or front root) → effector. A spinal nerve after the roots join is mixed (sensory + motor). Cutting a ventral root gives paralysis with intact sensation.
  • Classic reflexes. Knee-jerk (patellar) reflex: muscle spindle (stretch sensor in the muscle) → monosynaptic (one-synapse) connection onto the quadriceps motor neuron; reciprocal inhibition of the hamstrings (relaxing the opposing muscle) uses an inhibitory interneuron. Withdrawal + crossed-extensor reflex stiffens the opposite leg. Golgi tendon organs sense tension and relax the muscle under extreme load.
  • Brain regions and damage patterns. Cerebellum (coordination, balance), medulla (breathing, heart rate, blood pressure), hypothalamus (temperature, thirst, hunger; ventromedial lesion → overeating, lateral lesion → undereating), thalamus (relay for all senses except smell). Spinal cord: gray matter (cell bodies) inside, white matter (myelinated axons) outside, the opposite of the cerebral cortex. Lower motor neuron damage → atrophy (muscle wasting) and absent reflexes; complete cord transection (cut) → hyperreflexia (exaggerated reflexes) below the lesion after spinal shock.

Everyday example: Touching a hot stove. Your hand jerks back before you even feel the pain, because the spinal cord answers the alarm directly (reflex). A moment later the message reaches the brain and you think "ouch". The other leg stiffens so you do not fall (crossed extensor).

Worked example (step by step): A patient has weakness, atrophy and absent reflexes in one arm, with normal sensation.

  1. Absent reflexes + atrophy = the final motor wire to the muscle is damaged.
  2. That is the lower motor neuron (ventral horn or ventral root).
  3. Sensation is normal, so the dorsal (sensory) root is intact.

MCAT trap: Calling the knee-jerk reflex "no synapse" or "polysynaptic." It is monosynaptic (one sensory-to-motor synapse); relaxing the antagonist needs an interneuron, but the core reflex does not.

Concept 7: Sensory receptors and homeostatic sensors

In plain English: Sensory receptors turn things like light, touch, heat and chemicals into electrical signals. The brain knows what kind of sensation it is by which wire the signal arrives on. Some receptors also quietly monitor the body's blood pressure, oxygen and salt, and trigger automatic corrections.

Analogy: Sensory receptors are translators: each one listens to a single language (light, stretch, chemicals, heat) and converts it into the nervous system's only language, electrical signals. Some translators keep reporting forever (tonic); others report only changes and then go quiet (phasic, adapting).

Official definition: Sensory transduction converts a stimulus into a receptor potential (a graded change in Vm) that, if large enough, triggers action potentials; the perceived modality (type of sensation) depends on which pathway is activated (labeled line), not on the stimulus itself.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Graded receptor potentials and adaptation. Receptor potentials are graded and local; APs are all-or-none. Adaptation: constant pressure soon goes unnoticed as phasic receptors stop firing.
  • Labeled lines and receptor classes. Pressing on the eye makes you "see" light because the optic pathway always means vision. Classes: mechanoreceptors (touch, stretch), thermoreceptors, nociceptors (tissue damage, pain), photoreceptors (light), chemoreceptors, osmoreceptors (hypothalamus; thirst and ADH), proprioceptors (muscle spindles, joint receptors; limb position).
  • Homeostatic sensors. Arterial baroreceptors (pressure sensors in big arteries) fire less when blood pressure drops (standing up quickly) → less vagal and more sympathetic output → heart rate and vessel resistance rise. Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies in the neck) respond most to low arterial PO₂ (oxygen level) and also CO₂/H⁺; central chemoreceptors (in the brainstem) respond to CO₂, which crosses the blood–brain barrier and forms H⁺ in CSF.

Everyday example: Putting on a watch. You feel it at first, but a minute later you forget it is there: your touch receptors adapted. Take it off and you notice again, because receptors report changes.

Worked example (step by step): Someone stands up and mean arterial pressure falls from 93 to 80 mmHg.

  1. Less pressure → carotid sinus stretched less → baroreceptor firing decreases.
  2. The medulla reads this as "pressure low": it cuts parasympathetic (vagal) output and raises sympathetic output.
  3. Heart rate and vasoconstriction increase → pressure returns toward 93 mmHg within seconds.

MCAT trap: "Baroreceptors fire more when pressure falls." They are stretch receptors; less stretch means less firing.

Concept 8: The autonomic nervous system

In plain English: The autonomic nervous system runs your organs automatically: heart rate, digestion, pupils, sweating. It has two branches that usually push in opposite directions: sympathetic for emergencies and parasympathetic for rest. Most MCAT questions test which transmitter and receptor each branch uses.

Analogy: The autonomic system is a car's two pedals. Sympathetic is the gas (fight or flight: faster heart, wider airways, more glucose), parasympathetic is the brake (rest and digest: slower heart, more digestion). At rest the parasympathetic brake is gently on for the heart.

Official definition: The autonomic nervous system uses two-neuron efferent chains: sympathetic outflow is thoracolumbar (from the chest and lower-back spinal cord) with short preganglionic (first neuron) and long postganglionic (second neuron) fibers, usually releasing norepinephrine at targets; parasympathetic outflow is craniosacral (brainstem and lowest spinal cord) with long preganglionic and short postganglionic fibers releasing acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors. All preganglionic neurons release ACh onto nicotinic receptors.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Wiring. Sympathetic: thoracolumbar (T1–L2), short pre / long post (ganglia in the paravertebral chain beside the cord), NE at target (exception: sweat glands use ACh on muscarinic receptors). The adrenal medulla is a modified sympathetic ganglion: preganglionic ACh (nicotinic) triggers epinephrine release into blood. Parasympathetic: craniosacral, long pre / short post (ganglia in or near the organ), ACh; the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) carries most of it.
  • Receptors and effects. β1 (heart, ↑ rate and force; blocked by β1-blockers), β2 (opens airways; albuterol), α1 (narrows blood vessels), muscarinic (blocked by atropine → dry mouth, fast heart, dilated pupils, urinary retention). Sympathetic: pupil dilation, ↑ glycogenolysis (glycogen breakdown), ↓ digestion, ejaculation. Parasympathetic: erection ("point and shoot"), accommodation for near vision (ciliary muscle contraction), digestion.
  • Heart and gut. Intrinsic (built-in) heart rate ≈ 100 beats/min; resting rate ≈ 70 because vagal tone dominates. Most blood vessels are controlled mainly by sympathetic tone. The enteric nervous system (the gut's own nerve network) can run gut motility on its own.

Everyday example: Coasting a car downhill with a light foot on the brake. Lift your foot off the brake (cut the vagus) and the car speeds up to the speed the hill gives it (the heart's own 100 beats/min), even though you never touched the gas.

Worked example (step by step): The vagus nerves to an animal's heart are cut.

  1. At rest, vagal (parasympathetic) tone is the main influence, holding the rate at ~70.
  2. Cutting it removes the brake, exposing the SA node's intrinsic rate (~100 beats/min).
  3. Ganglionic blockade (both divisions off) does the same at rest, because vagal tone is the larger influence.

MCAT trap: Saying sympathetic postganglionic fibers always release NE. Sweat glands get ACh (muscarinic), and the adrenal medulla releases mainly epinephrine into the blood.

Concept 9: Hormone classes, receptors and second messengers

In plain English: Hormones come in two main styles. Water-soluble hormones (peptides, adrenaline) cannot cross the oily cell membrane, so they bind a receptor on the surface and set off a fast chain reaction inside. Fat-soluble hormones (steroids, thyroid hormone) slip through the membrane and change which genes are switched on, which is slower but lasts longer.

Analogy: Peptide hormones are visitors who cannot enter the building (water-soluble), so they ring the doorbell (surface receptor) and a chain of staff passes the message inside (second messengers): fast. Steroid hormones are staff with keys (lipid-soluble): they walk in, go straight to the manager's office (nucleus) and rewrite the instructions (gene transcription): slow but lasting.

Official definition: Peptide and catecholamine (adrenaline-family) hormones are water-soluble, bind cell-surface receptors and act through second messengers within seconds to minutes; steroid and thyroid hormones are lipid-soluble, travel bound to carrier proteins, bind intracellular receptors and alter gene transcription over hours.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Peptides vs. steroids vs. amines. Peptides (water-soluble, stored in vesicles, membrane receptors, second messengers, fast, short half-life). Steroids (made from cholesterol in smooth ER and mitochondria, not stored, diffuse out as made; carried on proteins, long half-life; intracellular receptors; change transcription, slow; blocked by actinomycin D, a drug that stops transcription). Amines: thyroid hormones act like steroids (nuclear receptors); catecholamines act like peptides.
  • Second-messenger chains. Gs → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A (glucagon on liver); phosphodiesterase breaks down cAMP (inhibiting it prolongs the signal). Gq → phospholipase C → IP₃ (Ca²⁺ release) + DAG (protein kinase C). Insulin uses a receptor tyrosine kinase (a receptor that is itself a kinase). Cascades amplify: a few receptors activate millions of enzymes.
  • Targeting and dose. Only cells with the receptor respond. Dose–response plateaus at receptor saturation (all receptors filled); chronic high hormone causes down-regulation (fewer receptors). Paracrine signals act on neighbors without entering blood.
Fraction remaining = (½)^(t / t½)

In plain words: after each half-life, half of what was left is cleared, so the fraction remaining is one-half multiplied by itself once for every half-life that has passed.

When to use it: questions giving a hormone's or drug's half-life and asking how much is left after a time, or how long until a certain fraction remains ("t½ = 10 min, how much after 30 min"). When it does not apply: it assumes clearance in proportion to the amount present (first-order) and no new secretion or dosing during the time. t and t½ must be in the same unit.

  2. Fraction = (½)³ = 1/8.
  3. 0.125 (12.5%) remains.

MCAT trap: Subtracting linearly ("half gone in 10 min, so all gone in 20"). Each half-life removes half of what is left.

Concept 10: Hypothalamic–pituitary axes and feedback

In plain English: The hypothalamus (in the brain) tells the pituitary gland (just below it) which hormones to release, and the pituitary in turn tells other glands (thyroid, adrenals, ovaries, testes) what to do. The final hormone then signals back to turn the chain down, like a thermostat. Reading which levels are high or low tells you where a disease is.

Analogy: The hypothalamus is the CEO, the anterior pituitary is the middle manager, and the target glands are the workers. The CEO sends memos by private courier (the portal system), the manager passes orders on (tropic hormones), and when the workers' output is high enough the CEO and manager slow down (negative feedback), like a thermostat.

Official definition: Hypothalamic releasing hormones travel via the hypophyseal portal system (a private set of blood vessels from hypothalamus to pituitary) to the anterior pituitary, which secretes TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, GH and prolactin; the posterior pituitary releases ADH and oxytocin made by hypothalamic neurons; most axes are controlled by negative feedback from the final hormone.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Front vs. back pituitary. Hypothalamus → anterior pituitary (portal system) for TSH (thyroid-stimulating), ACTH (adrenal-stimulating), FSH, LH (sex glands), GH (growth hormone), prolactin (milk). Posterior pituitary releases ADH and oxytocin made in the hypothalamus (it holds the axon terminals; neural tissue). Stalk compression lowers most anterior hormones but raises prolactin (dopamine inhibition lost).
  • Feedback types. Most axes use negative feedback; oxytocin in labor (and milk ejection) and the LH surge (driven by high estrogen) are positive feedback. GnRH must be pulsatile (released in bursts); continuous GnRH down-regulates LH/FSH.
  • Diagnose by pattern. High final hormone + low tropic hormone → primary gland problem; high both → source upstream (pituitary or ectopic, meaning a tumor elsewhere making the hormone). Low final + high tropic → gland failure (primary hypothyroidism, Addison disease). Low both + no response to releasing hormone → pituitary defect. Exogenous (taken as medicine) hormone (prednisone, T₄, anabolic steroids) suppresses the axis.

Everyday example: A home thermostat and furnace. When the room is cold (low hormone), the thermostat (hypothalamus/pituitary) keeps calling for heat (high TSH). If the furnace is broken (the thyroid), the thermostat calls louder and louder but the room stays cold: low output + high command = the furnace is the problem.

Worked example (step by step): Lab results: low T₄, high TSH.

  1. T₄ (final hormone) is low, so negative feedback on the pituitary is weak.
  2. The pituitary responds normally by raising TSH. So the pituitary works.
  3. The gland itself fails → primary hypothyroidism.
  4. Contrast: low T₄, low TSH, and TRH injection gives no TSH rise → pituitary (secondary) defect.

MCAT trap: Exogenous steroids raise ACTH. Giving glucocorticoids suppresses CRH and ACTH by negative feedback, so the adrenal cortex atrophies. Stopping them suddenly causes adrenal insufficiency.

Concept 11: Fuel control: insulin, glucagon, cortisol and epinephrine

In plain English: Your body keeps blood sugar in a narrow range. After you eat, insulin tells cells to take sugar in and store it. Between meals and during stress, glucagon, adrenaline and cortisol release stored sugar or make new sugar. Diabetes is what happens when the insulin side fails.

Analogy: Blood glucose is a bank account. Insulin is the saver: after a meal it deposits glucose into muscle, fat and liver. Glucagon, epinephrine and cortisol are withdrawers: during fasting or stress they pull glucose back out (from liver glycogen and new glucose synthesis).

Official definition: Insulin from pancreatic β cells lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake (GLUT4 insertion in muscle and fat) and storage; glucagon from α cells raises it by stimulating hepatic (liver) glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis (making new glucose from non-sugar molecules); somatostatin from δ cells inhibits both; cortisol and epinephrine are counter-regulatory hormones that raise glucose.

Core idea (3 points):

  • The pancreas trio. Insulin (β cells, ↓ glucose): inserts GLUT4 (a glucose doorway protein) into muscle and fat membranes; most neurons use insulin-independent GLUT1/GLUT3. Glucagon (α cells, ↑ glucose) acts mainly on the liver. Somatostatin (δ cells) inhibits both. Insulin and glucagon are antagonists (opposites).
  • Stress hormones. Cortisol (↑ glucose via gluconeogenesis, immunosuppression; highest in the early morning) and epinephrine (fight or flight; glycogenolysis, lipolysis (fat breakdown) via hormone-sensitive lipase; sympathetic tone suppresses insulin during exercise so glucose stays available). Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) → glucagon + epinephrine first, then cortisol and GH.
  • Diabetes types. Type 1: autoimmune (the immune system attacks) β-cell loss, no insulin → unchecked lipolysis and ketone production (ketoacidosis, acid buildup in the blood). Type 2: insulin resistance (receptors present but poor response), often with high insulin early.

Everyday example: A household budget. Payday (a meal) brings in money; you deposit what you do not need into savings (insulin → glycogen and fat). During a lean month (fasting) you withdraw from savings to keep the checking account (blood sugar) at the same level (glucagon). An emergency (stress) triggers a big, quick withdrawal (epinephrine) and a longer belt-tightening plan (cortisol).

Worked example (step by step): Track an overnight fast and then breakfast.

  1. Overnight, glucose drifts down → insulin falls, glucagon rises.
  2. Liver glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis keep glucose ≈ 4–5 mM (70–90 mg/dL; 90/18 = 5 mM).
  3. Thirty minutes after a carbohydrate meal the pattern reverses: insulin up, glucagon down, GLUT4 moves to muscle and fat membranes.

MCAT trap: "Insulin is needed for glucose to enter all cells." Brain neurons, red cells and liver take up glucose without insulin; GLUT4 tissues (skeletal muscle, fat) depend on it.

Concept 12: Water, salt and calcium balance

In plain English: Hormones keep the right amount of water, salt and calcium in your blood. ADH saves water, aldosterone saves salt (and water follows it), ANP dumps both when there is too much, and PTH and vitamin D raise blood calcium while calcitonin lowers it.

Analogy: The body's water tank has two valves. ADH is the water valve (keep water, concentrate urine). Aldosterone is the salt valve (keep Na⁺, water follows). ANP is the overflow alarm that opens both drains when the tank is too full. Calcium has its own thermostat: PTH and vitamin D raise it, calcitonin lowers it.

Official definition: ADH (antidiuretic hormone, made in the hypothalamus, released from the posterior pituitary) inserts aquaporins (water channels) in collecting-duct cells of the kidney; aldosterone (zona glomerulosa) increases Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion in principal cells and is driven by the renin–angiotensin system; ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide, from the heart) opposes both; PTH (parathyroid hormone) raises blood Ca²⁺ via bone, kidney and calcitriol (active vitamin D), while calcitonin from thyroid C cells lowers it.

Core idea (3 points):

  • Water vs. salt. Rising plasma osmolarity → osmoreceptors → ADH → more water reabsorbed (concentrated urine). ADH changes water alone (lowers osmolarity); aldosterone changes Na⁺ and water together (raises volume, not osmolarity). Alcohol inhibits ADH (diuresis, more urine). Excess ADH (SIADH) → dilute plasma (hyponatremia, low blood sodium), concentrated urine. Central diabetes insipidus (no ADH made) responds to desmopressin (a man-made ADH).
  • Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone. Low kidney blood flow → juxtaglomerular cells release renin → angiotensin I → (ACE, angiotensin-converting enzyme) angiotensin II → aldosterone + vasoconstriction. ACE inhibitors raise renin and angiotensin I, lower angiotensin II and aldosterone. Primary hyperaldosteronism: high blood pressure, low K⁺, low renin. Atrial stretch → ANP → natriuresis (salt loss in urine). Adrenal cortex zones: glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol), reticularis (androgens).
  • Calcium. PTH ↑ Ca²⁺ (bone resorption, kidney Ca²⁺ reabsorption, phosphate excretion, activates calcitriol); calcitriol ↑ gut Ca²⁺ absorption; calcitonin (thyroid C cells) ↓ Ca²⁺. High Ca²⁺ + high PTH + low phosphate → primary hyperparathyroidism; high Ca²⁺ + low PTH → non-parathyroid cause. Chronic kidney disease → low calcitriol and phosphate retention → secondary ↑ PTH. Accidental parathyroid removal → hypocalcemia (tingling, spasms).
Plasma osmolality ≈ 2[Na⁺] + [glucose]/18 + [BUN]/2.8

In plain words: to estimate how concentrated the blood is, count sodium twice (once for itself and once for the negative ion that travels with it), then add glucose and urea after converting them from mg/dL into the same mmol units.

When to use it: questions giving blood sodium, glucose and BUN and asking for plasma osmolality, whether a patient is dehydrated or overhydrated, or whether ADH and thirst will be triggered. When it does not apply: it is an estimate. Unmeasured particles (alcohol, poisons such as ethylene glycol) make the measured value higher than the calculated one (the "osmolal gap"). The ÷18 and ÷2.8 apply only when glucose and BUN are in mg/dL; in mmol/L just add them.

Concept 13: Thyroid, growth, reproductive and other glands; neuroendocrine integration

In plain English: Several other glands set your metabolism, growth, reproduction, sleep and appetite. The nervous system and the hormone system work as a team: nerves give fast, short, targeted responses, hormones give slower, body-wide, longer-lasting ones, and the hypothalamus links the two.

Analogy: If the nervous system is a text message (instant, private, short), the endocrine system is a broadcast email (slower, reaches everyone with the right inbox, effects last). The hypothalamus is the person who types both.

Official definition: Thyroid hormones (T₃/T₄) raise basal metabolic rate (energy burned at rest) and are required for normal development; growth hormone acts largely via IGF-1; gonadal (sex gland) steroids and the pituitary gonadotropins (FSH, LH) control reproduction; other glands (pineal, thymus, kidney, adipose, gut) secrete hormones; nervous and endocrine systems are integrated through neuroendocrine cells of the hypothalamus (neurons that release hormones).

Core idea (3 points):

  • Thyroid. T₃/T₄ ↑ metabolic rate and heat (hyperthyroid: heat intolerance, weight loss, fast heart); Graves disease antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor (high T₄, low TSH). Iodine deficiency → low T₄ → high TSH → goiter (enlarged thyroid). Congenital (from birth) hypothyroidism impairs brain development. T₃ increases β-receptors (permissive effect on epinephrine: it lets epinephrine work fully).
  • Growth and reproduction. GH → IGF-1 (made by the liver) → bone and cartilage growth; after the growth plates close, excess GH causes acromegaly, not taller height. Leydig cells make testosterone (driven by LH); Sertoli cells make inhibin (inhibits FSH). The corpus luteum (left-over follicle after ovulation) makes progesterone; hCG from the embryo rescues it in early pregnancy. Menopause: no ovarian feedback → high FSH and LH. Puberty starts with rising GnRH pulses. Androgen insensitivity: XY, female external genitalia, high testosterone.
  • Other glands and integration. Pineal (melatonin; light → retina → SCN, the brain's clock → less melatonin), thymus (T-cell maturation), kidney (EPO, which makes red cells, rises at high altitude), adipose (leptin = "I'm full"), stomach (ghrelin = "I'm hungry"). Sympathetic responses act in seconds, HPA cortisol over minutes to hours; nervous signals are faster, more targeted and shorter-lived than endocrine signals. Endocrine disruptors are outside chemicals that bind hormone receptors (e.g. estrogen receptors in the nucleus).

Everyday example: A cold house in winter. Fast fix (seconds): you put on a sweater and shiver (nerves). Slow fix (days): you turn up the furnace's baseline setting for the season (thyroid hormone raises metabolic rate). Same goal, two time scales.

Worked example (step by step): A person is moved into the cold.

  1. Fast response (seconds): sympathetic vasoconstriction (skin vessels narrow to save heat) and shivering (somatic motor).
  2. Slow response (days): TRH → TSH → more T₄/T₃ → higher basal metabolic rate.
  3. The two systems hand off the same goal, keeping core temperature near 37 °C.

MCAT trap: Expecting GH excess in adults to increase height. Once epiphyseal (growth) plates fuse, bones grow in width only (hands, jaw, feet: acromegaly).

Pathway: HPA axis with negative feedback

Ion events in an action potential

C) 3 MCAT-STYLE PRACTICE QUESTIONS

Q1. A toxin blocks voltage-gated K⁺ channels in a neuron. Which change in the action potential is most likely?

  • A) It fails to reach threshold
  • B) Its repolarization is prolonged
  • C) Its peak amplitude falls to −20 mV
  • D) The resting potential becomes more negative

Answer: B. Without voltage-gated K⁺ efflux, repolarization depends on slower mechanisms, so the spike is wider.

  • A is wrong: reaching threshold depends on Na⁺ channels.
  • B is correct: K⁺ channels drive repolarization.
  • C is wrong: peak amplitude is set by Na⁺ influx (toward E_Na).
  • D is wrong: resting potential is set mostly by K⁺ leak channels, which are not voltage-gated; blocking K⁺ channels would, if anything, depolarize rest.

Q2. A patient has high cortisol and low ACTH. Where is the primary problem most likely located?

  • A) Anterior pituitary adenoma secreting ACTH
  • B) Adrenal tumor secreting cortisol
  • C) Hypothalamic CRH deficiency
  • D) Ectopic ACTH from a lung tumor

Answer: B. Autonomous cortisol suppresses ACTH by negative feedback.

  • A is wrong: a pituitary source would raise ACTH.
  • B is correct: high hormone + low upstream signal points to the gland itself.
  • C is wrong: CRH deficiency would lower both ACTH and cortisol.
  • D is wrong: ectopic ACTH would raise ACTH.

Q3. A drug blocks nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at autonomic ganglia. Which effect on the heart is expected at rest, when parasympathetic tone dominates?

  • A) Heart rate falls
  • B) Heart rate rises
  • C) No change, because the heart uses muscarinic receptors
  • D) Heart stops

Answer: B. Ganglionic blockade cuts both divisions; removing the dominant vagal (parasympathetic) brake raises heart rate toward the SA node's intrinsic rate (≈ 100 beats/min).

  • A is wrong: the sympathetic input is also blocked, but at rest the larger loss is vagal tone.
  • B is correct: loss of dominant parasympathetic tone.
  • C is wrong: the heart's muscarinic receptors are postganglionic; the drug blocks the ganglion upstream.
  • D is wrong: the SA node is autorhythmic and keeps firing without autonomic input.
